prize_parts.citation: For the development of ligand-controlled palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, which made the formation of aryl-nitrogen bonds a general and routine operation in organic synthesis.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Buchwald and Hartwig for Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling. The chair asked what this citation says that the 2010 prize does not. The 2010 prize recognised C-C bond formation between organometallic partners and organic halides. C-N coupling required a different mechanistic solution: amine binding and deprotonation to an amido-palladium species, and C-N reductive elimination, which is intrinsically slow and competes with beta-hydride elimination. It became practical only through ligand design (chelating bisphosphines, then bulky dialkylbiaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines), a separate body of chemical insight. Its adoption is verifiable in commercial ligand and precatalyst families, in a large share of medicinal-chemistry and process routes to aryl amines, and in materials such as OLED hole-transport layers. The attribution is two names, the credit is independent and simultaneous, and thirty years of use leave no question of maturity. Having heard the round, I still find no other shortlisted entry that combines a clear chemical advance, a clean cut at three people or fewer and unquestioned maturity, though I accept the committee may weigh breadth of impact differently.
statement.case_against: The principal objection remains that a committee may see C-N coupling as the sequel to the 2010 prize. I think the mechanistic and ligand-design argument answers it, but it is a judgement and two colleagues (Aqvist, Brzezinski) say expert reports should settle it. A second weakness is political: nobody besides me prefers B052, and Aqvist keeps it only as a reserve. I should not mistake isolation for lack of merit, but a prize that cannot reach five votes cannot be awarded, and I have tried to be honest about which alternatives I could live with. Finally, the 'routine tool' framing favours methodology over discovery, and a committee that prizes new phenomena over enabling chemistry would rank it lower.

responses.point: Aqvist agrees Buchwald and Hartwig are the right pair if the topic is chosen, but keeps B052 as a reserve because the 2010 cross-coupling prize already rewarded Pd-catalysed bond making and the committee would have to argue for a new bond type and ligand logic.
responses.response: That is the right test and I will try to meet it concretely. The 2010 citation was about C-C coupling with organometallic nucleophiles, where transmetalation and C-C reductive elimination are facile. In C-N coupling the amine is a poor transmetalating partner, the amido complexes are prone to beta-hydride elimination, and C-N reductive elimination from Pd(II) had no precedent that made it dependable. Solving this required new ligand classes and mechanistic work, not application of the earlier recipe. I would also be happy for the citation to name the bond and the ligand design explicitly, so that the prize is plainly distinct. I accept this is where the committee will make or break the case and I have no new evidence beyond the argument.

responses.point: Brzezinski accepts that maturity is beyond question for B052 but asks whether a different bond construction with a different ligand logic is a new achievement or a sequel, and wants expert reports to answer it before ranking it over a discovery with no prior prize in the area.
responses.response: I agree the expert reports should answer this and I would not object if they decide against me. My practical test is whether chemists had to learn something new: they did, and the proof is that the ligands developed for amination are not the ones used in Suzuki or Heck couplings. On B062, I respect the rigour of Gray and Winkler and the compact attribution, but I share your concern that it completes the story of the 1992 Marcus prize more than it opens a new one. Of the two sequel questions, I think B052 has the stronger answer because it needed new catalysts, whereas tunnelling through proteins applies an existing rate theory to a new medium, albeit with elegant experiments.

responses.point: Linke argues that B016 is the clearest chain of credit (Miyasaka, Park, Snaith) and that the prize concerns the discovery of the absorber and a decade of replication, not product deployment, while accepting that Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis have credible claims.
responses.response: You asked directly whether the trio is acceptable and whether stability should make us wait. I do not dispute the efficiency numbers or the replication, and I accept that a prize need not wait for modules. My difficulty is two-fold. First, the chain from Gratzel's dye cells through Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Seok and Kanatzidis is long enough that I do not trust any trio to survive scrutiny without the priority reports. Second, I still judge the novelty mainly as materials and device physics, and I would want the citation to say what chemical insight, for instance defect chemistry or composition tuning, is being honoured. If the reports back the trio and the citation is chemical, I could support B016, so I will not rank it below my alternatives out of reflex.

responses.point: Sparr defends B069 by separating the well-established thermodynamic framework of condensates (multivalency, saturation concentration, coexistence) from disputed in vivo cases, and says the citation must be worded around the physical principle to stay in chemistry.
responses.response: That distinction is helpful and moves me a little: a framework written in terms of phase diagrams and valency is physical chemistry, and I accept your argument that disputed individual assemblies are normal for a young field. It does not fully answer my question about what was new chemically. The liquid behaviour of P granules is a cell-biological observation, and the sequence-level physical chemistry that makes the principle quantitative is largely Pappu's and Mittag's, whom the Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen trio omits. You have said omitting them is a worry too. So I would consider B069 only with a different and chemically defined cut, and for now it remains behind my alternatives.

responses.point: Aili prefers B045 with Cullis and Langer, arguing that approved siRNA products and billions of mRNA vaccine doses show demonstrated impact, and that the lipidoid and combinatorial strand made delivery general.
responses.response: Of the large-impact entries, B045 is the one I find most persuasive as chemistry, because pKa-tuned ionizable lipids are a molecular design solution. That is why it replaces B020 among my alternatives. But the chair's question about who holds the decisive step is unresolved for me. Sparr's reading that the ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing line is decisive is closer to my own sense of the chemistry than adding Langer, and her trio (Cullis, Hope, Madden) is at least a coherent cut, but you and she disagree on exactly the point that decides it. I also want to see the 2023 Medicine prize addressed in the citation wording.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats C-N coupling as distinct from the 2010 prize; the expert reports on this are decisive and I have not seen them.
Priority and credit details for early tin amide chemistry (Kosugi, Migita) and for the first catalytic aminations, which I am working from memory.
Whether any single configuration can reach five votes; B016 and B045 have broader support than B052, and I may need to move my vote toward one of them.
For B045, whether Cullis with Hope and Madden or with Langer is the right cut; for B012, which two names are non-negotiable.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known institutional or collaborative tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or other credited persons on the shortlist. My synthetic-methodology background favours B052 and I flag this bias. I share Lund with Linke and Sparr, which I do not consider a recusal issue for these candidates.
